//: Development overrides for running the gateway outside Docker.
Compose service names only resolve on the compose network, so a gateway
started with 'dotnet run' cannot reach 'invoice-service'. This file repoints
the same routes at localhost and the published ports.
The routes are repeated in full rather than patched. .NET configuration
merges JSON arrays by index, so a partial override would silently depend on
the two files keeping their routes in the same order. Repeating the array
makes the override total and obvious; if the two drift apart, the failure is
a routing 404 rather than a request quietly going to the wrong service.
//OperatorRoutes: The SOC console and the ask page, added so that alerts are DISPLAYED
rather than read as Swagger JSON. Two decisions are worth recording.
First, every one of these routes carries an explicit RateLimitOptions
block, as every other route does. With a global ClientIdHeader set,
Ocelot applies a default empty rule to any route that does not opt out,
then cannot identify the client and answers 503. Omitting the block is
the bug that silently broke /api/rates, /api/auth/login and
/api/checkout for a whole day on day 7.
Second, what is NOT routed here is deliberate:
POST /api/soc/events is the ingestion path. Services reach it
directly on the compose network. Exposing it through the gateway
would let anyone inject fabricated security events into the system's
own evidence, which is the one thing this phase has to be
trustworthy about. GET /api/soc/events is routed; POST is not, and
Ocelot matches on method as well as path, so a POST here is a 404
at the gateway.
/api/graph/load/* and /api/graph/evaluate rebuild and benchmark the
graph. They are operator jobs run deliberately against port 5006,
not something a browser page should be able to trigger.
The honest gap: these routes sit behind the same API key as the
payment endpoints, so any merchant's key can read the whole platform
alert feed. The system has no operator role to check instead. The
report says so rather than hiding it.

//RateLimitOptions: Client identity comes from X-Merchant-Id, which the gateway sets itself
after validating the API key, so the quota is per MERCHANT rather than
per key or per IP. A merchant with three keys shares one quota, which is
the honest unit: the limit protects the platform from one customer, not
from one credential. Per-IP would lump every merchant behind a corporate
Limits apply to the invoice write path and to the operator routes that
serve the SOC console. Rates are public market data that a checkout
page polls legitimately every few seconds.
Note the gap this leaves: unauthenticated requests are rejected by the
API key middleware before Ocelot ever sees them, so they carry no
X-Merchant-Id and are never rate limited here. Someone brute forcing keys
is throttled by nothing at this layer. Every rejection is logged as
API_KEY_INVALID with its source address, so the SOC layer can see it, but
detection is not prevention and the report says so.
